dispositions.rationale: A renderer that returns cached prose for a new record is an invented implementation defect, not an in-scope failure the document names; CR-R7 pins determinism and the golden fixtures pin the mapping from record to output. An unsupported implementation prescription earns no criterion (restraint).

CR-D1's non-drift claim is about facts the two artifacts share, each of which is one record field rendered twice; the decision's wording now says so. Agreement of meaning between two author-written prose fields is not mechanically decidable and is the author's and the rewrite pass's (restraint).

Whether the prose carries the promised content is a judgment no check over the record can decide; the form, length and required references are pinned and the content is the author's, read in review as today (restraint, can-fail).

Section 3.4 assigns this writing rule to the author and the rewrite pass and says the lint enforces only what it can decide. The rule is not mechanically decidable, and CR-W8 is the human-judgment criterion over the applied prose with a recorded basis per rule. A criterion for an undecidable rule earns none (restraint).

How many scripts implement the renderer is an implementation prescription, not an observable obligation; the golden fixtures and CR-L17 pin the behaviour. Restraint.

publish calls gh with the ambient credential, the author's login; the reviewing App's token is reached only through prgroom's own code, which this skill neither imports nor invokes. Which account is logged in is a property of the session, not of the skill, and CR-D8 records the split (restraint).

The meaning check is the author's by CR-D6, which says the script cannot tell a reported check from a verified claim; CR-W8 is the human-judgment criterion that records that check against the fixtures with a basis per rule. A mechanical criterion for an undecidable check earns none (restraint).

CR-W9 makes the record admit one application per author revision; how many times an agent dispatches an editor before applying is agent behaviour outside the artifacts, which no check over them can decide (observable-obligation, restraint).

Slice W's item takes a dependency edge on agents-config-9k9.486 at minting, as section 7 now states, so the tracker refuses to make it ready before the ruling; that is the gate, and it is the tracker's, not a criterion of this spec (restraint).

The escalation rule is a policy the owner applies to the series the record carries (CR-W10); applying it is an owner decision outside the artifacts, which no check over them can decide (observable-obligation, restraint).

The admit-request gate is the repository's standing rule for any new skill, recorded on the slice's work item as slice L's preamble states; a criterion restating a standing rule the tracker already evidences earns none (restraint).

parts.statement: The tested subject violations are refused, including excessive length, invalid type, absent or tracker-shaped component, and an absent or incorrect short id; the tested 100-character valid subject passes.

Fixture commits omit tables, details, fences and HTML comments, and the tested commit-prose markup cases are refused.
Why contains two or three sentences and Change contains three or four.
The complete rendered nontrivial body, including its human work-item line and labels, remains within 80–150 words.
A trivial commit renders without the optional prose body while retaining all required trailers.

obligations.statement: Commit messages follow the subject, body and trailer contract, including the trivial-change variant.

Each finding that changed code or prose has exactly one reply, including changed findings marked Superseded.

ground.reason: CR-W5 requires every applied response to bump the record's revision, so after a successful pass the latest rewrite entry names the base revision, one behind the current one. CR-W9's refusal condition, which fires only when the latest entry names the current revision, can then never hold, yet its own check requires the second application to be refused. The rule statement, the bump and the check cannot all hold together.

objections.objection: The rewrite-pass admission rule is dead as written. CR-W9 says each rewrite entry records the base revision the application was made against, and refuses a second application only when the latest entry names the record's current revision. CR-W5's apply bumps the revision, so after a successful pass the entry names the base, never the current revision, and the refusal can never fire. The criterion's check then demands a refusal no stated rule produces.

scenario.expect: CR-W5 and CR-W9's entry rule require the response to apply and bump again, because the latest entry names 4 and not the current revision 5. CR-W9's check requires the same input to be refused. The set demands both verdicts on one response, and an implementer must invent a semantics the text does not state, such as recording the resulting revision instead of the base.
scenario.given: A record at revision 5 after one applied rewrite pass. The latest rewrite entry records base revision 4, and CR-W5's bump moved the record to 5.
scenario.when: apply-prose receives a fresh, structurally valid response whose record and section digests match the revision-5 record.

ground.reason: CR-C5 omits the replace-the-None. clause that CR-C3 states for its own case, so the set leaves the join-or-replace decision open. Under the join reading the generator's own output fails CR-L11, and CR-C5's check cases never exercise the None. heads_up state that would settle it.

objections.objection: CR-C5 adds a heads_up row when the latest round is not terminal-clean, but unlike CR-C3 for the no-envelope case it never says whether that row replaces the single None. entry. The join reading makes the campaign generator emit a record that CR-L11 fails: None. beside another entry.

scenario.expect: Read as a join, the record holds None. beside the new row and CR-L11 fails it, so the tool ships a record its own lint rejects. Read as a replace, parallel to CR-C3, the record is lint-clean. The wording admits both outcomes, and the decision it blocks is whether the generator must always replace the None. entry or may join it.
scenario.given: A record whose heads_up holds the single None. entry, and a campaign whose latest round carries a mechanical finding, so the terminal sha is empty per CR-C5.
scenario.when: The campaign generator writes the heads_up row saying the latest round is not terminal-clean.

ground.reason: CR-P9 keys a merge refusal on a comparison whose empty case the set defines (CR-C5's empty terminal sha) but never covers, and gates it on a presence test the set never defines for the empty campaign CR-C3 describes. Each reading gives the merge command different reach, and no other criterion decides between them.

objections.objection: CR-P9 makes merge refuse when the live head differs from the campaign's terminal sha when a campaign is present, but CR-C5 makes an empty terminal sha a normal state and CR-C3 makes an empty campaign a normal state. What a comparison against an empty sha means, and whether an empty campaign counts as present, decide whether an unreviewed or not-yet-clean PR can merge.

scenario.expect: Reading the comparison literally, the empty terminal sha differs from the live head and merge refuses, so no PR merges before a terminal-clean round exists. Reading the comparison as skipped when the field is empty, or the empty campaign as not present, merge proceeds on a head no round accepted. The two readings produce opposite verdicts on one merge.
scenario.given: A PR whose campaign holds one halted round. The terminal sha field is empty per CR-C5, and the live head equals the record's head sha.
scenario.when: The author runs merge on the PR.

ground.reason: The criteria test the caveat row being added and the None. entry being replaced (CR-C3, CR-C5), and a second run only over unchanged comments (CR-C6). objections.objection: A campaign-written heads_up caveat survives the condition that justified it, so the published one-pager carries a false caveat. The heads_up group is not a generated group and its entries are x-rewritable, so the generator cannot even find its own row by wording to remove it.

scenario.expect: the stale caveat row is gone from heads_up and the terminal sha is set. No criterion checks the row's removal, so the body can assert both 'Terminal-clean at <sha>' and the stale caveat saying the latest round is not terminal-clean.

objections.objection: Lint accepts a record whose commit subject disagrees with the record's own type and component, so the PR body and the commit message, the two artifacts CR-D1 says cannot drift because they render from one record, disagree.

scenario.expect: a refusal naming the disagreement between the subject's type or component and the record's pr.type or pr.component. No criterion checks it, the body takes the docs variant with no Criteria section, and the merge commit's subject says feat.
scenario.given: a record whose pr.type is docs and whose pr.component is review-panel, with a commit subject 'feat(installer): …' of otherwise valid form
scenario.when: lint validates the record and render produces the body and the commit message

ground.reason: The document governs the PR body only as publish's output. The body that gh pr create needs, before any record comment exists, is neither specified nor tested, and the render's pointer line cannot name a comment that has not been posted.

objections.objection: The PR opens with a body no criterion governs, and if publish is forgotten the ungoverned body is the one the owner reads and the merge carries.

scenario.expect: a defined creation-time body, either the render without the pointer line or a named stub, that the checks tie to the record. The document names the record as the body's source and lint as the check before gh pr create, but no criterion pins what the body says between creation and the first publish.
scenario.given: a record that passes lint, and no pull request yet
scenario.when: the author creates the PR with gh pr create, before any record comment exists
